input:
Scope
This review sets out to cover catalysts for the hydrogenation of carbon dioxide, that is, the conversion of carbon dioxide with hydrogen to products including methanol, methane, dimethyl ether, and higher hydrocarbons. In total, the review covers 93 papers from the last 8 years. Papers are included where a catalyst is tested under flowing carbon dioxide and hydrogen and where both conversion and product selectivity are reported; studies of the water-gas shift reaction alone, and studies that report activity without selectivity, fall outside the review. The catalysts themselves fall into families that recur across the period: copper-based catalysts carried on oxide supports, catalysts based on indium oxide, noble-metal catalysts on oxide carriers, and zeolite-containing combinations that couple methanol formation to further conversion. It is important to note that conditions vary widely across the set. Temperature, pressure, feed ratio, and space velocity are seldom the same in any two papers, and the products targeted differ, so the review compares catalysts within product groups and treats comparisons across groups as comparisons of reported performance under unlike conditions, rather than as rankings of the materials themselves. Characterisation, it should also be noted, is reported unevenly across the set. Most papers support their performance claims with measurements of surface area and of the state of the active phase before and after reaction, but the measurements are not made on a common plan, and a catalyst described in one paper by its preparation alone cannot fairly be set against a catalyst described in another by its working surface. The review therefore records, for each paper, the characterisation actually reported, and does not infer the working state of a catalyst from its preparation where the paper does not measure that state.

Established results
Several results are reported consistently enough across the literature to be regarded as established. Carbon dioxide hydrogenation over copper-based catalysts produces methanol together with carbon monoxide from the reverse water-gas shift reaction, and the split between the two moves with temperature: higher temperature favours carbon monoxide, and methanol selectivity falls as conversion rises. Water is formed in both routes, and water inhibits the reaction on most catalysts tested; papers that remove water, or that feed it deliberately, show the rate and the selectivity responding in the direction that inhibition predicts. Promoters change the performance of a base catalyst in reproducible directions within a family, although the size of the change is specific to the preparation. Supports, moreover, are not inert: the same active metal on different oxide carriers gives different conversions at the same stated conditions, and the difference is attributed across the literature to the interface between the metal and the carrier, to the dispersion the carrier stabilises, and to acid or basic sites the carrier contributes. For indium oxide catalysts, the established picture is one of high methanol selectivity at low conversion, with activity limited by the supply of the surface vacancies the mechanism requires. Zeolite combinations convert the methanol formed on the first function into dimethyl ether or hydrocarbons, and their reported product distributions are set jointly by the two functions and by how closely the two are mixed.

Disagreements
Reports conflict on methanol selectivity at a stated conversion. One set of papers reports selectivity falling steeply as conversion rises, and reads the trend as the reverse water-gas shift overtaking methanol formation along the bed. Another set reports selectivity holding nearly constant across the same conversion range, and reads its result as the two routes running in parallel at rates fixed by the inlet conditions. The conflict is not resolved by the reported conditions, because the two sets differ in how conversion was changed: the first set changed temperature, while the second changed space velocity, and temperature moves the equilibrium and the shift reaction together while space velocity does not. Reports also conflict on the state of the copper surface under reaction, with one group assigning activity to metallic copper and another to copper at the interface with the support oxide, and the conflict rests on measurements made after reaction rather than during it. A third disagreement concerns deactivation: sintering is named as the cause in some reports and the accumulation of surface species in others, and the two are seldom separated, because the measurements that would separate them do not form part of the standard test.

Gaps
The measurement nobody reports is performance over extended time on stream. Tests in the reviewed set are short, and conversion and selectivity are reported at the start of the run or as an average over it; no paper tracks both quantities across a long continuous run under a feed that contains the water the reaction produces, so the deactivation behaviour that decides industrial use is largely absent from the record the review covers. Regeneration is treated in much the same way: a catalyst is sometimes reported as regenerated, but its conversion and selectivity after regeneration are not reported against the fresh values, so recovery is asserted rather than measured. A second gap is the absence of a common test protocol. Because feed composition, pressure, and space velocity are chosen paper by paper, the cross-paper comparisons this review is forced to make carry the condition differences with them, and the literature does not contain the shared-condition dataset that would remove them. Rates, furthermore, are reported on unlike bases, per mass of catalyst in some papers and per mass of active metal in others, which blocks the direct comparison of activity across families.
